# Nanolog: Java logging without logger fields

**Nanolog** is a zero-dependency logging library for Java 8+: every call goes through
the static methods of `LOG`, the source class is detected automatically, so no class
needs a logger field. It prints to the console, writes JSON lines, captures entries
in tests, and works on its own or on top of **SLF4J**, and therefore on top of
Logback, Log4j 2, JBoss Logging and others.

Nanolog for Java (`com.nanolaba:nanolog`) is not related to [NanoLog](https://github.com/PlatformLab/NanoLog), the nanosecond-scale logger for C++.

## Why Nanolog

- **Print debugging that names its values.** `LOG.dbg(order.total())` prints `order.total() = 129.90 (BigDecimal)` with the file and line of the call and returns the value, like `dbg!` in Rust and icecream in Python; see [Print debugging](#print-debugging-logdbg-prints-the-expression-and-its-value).
- **No logger fields.** `LOG.info("...")` works from any class; the caller is found by walking the stack.
- **Zero dependencies.** No transitive libraries; `slf4j-api` is needed only if you use `Slf4jLogger`.
- **SLF4J-style placeholders.** `{}` with escaping, array rendering and sane handling of missing or extra arguments.
- **JSON lines and tests built in.** `JsonLogger` writes one JSON object per line for `jq` and log collectors; `MemoryLogger` captures entries in a test and asserts on them, with the whole log in the failure message; see [JsonLogger](#jsonlogger) and [MemoryLogger and CompositeLogger](#memorylogger-and-compositelogger).
- **Levels change at run time.** `LOG.setLevel("com.acme.payments", DEBUG)` from an admin endpoint or a test takes effect in every thread, and `LOG.withLevel(...)` puts the old level back when the block ends; see [Changing levels at run time](#changing-levels-at-run-time).
- **Logging never throws.** A broken `toString()` becomes `[FAILED toString()]` instead of an exception in your code.
- **Lazy messages.** `LOG.debug(() -> ...)` is evaluated only when the level is enabled.
- **Pluggable.** A custom backend is one lambda or one class implementing `ILogger`.
- **Fits the agent loop.** One line per log call, output from the first run, an API that fits in one context window; see [Agent-driven development](#agent-driven-development).

The whole library:

```
logging
├── CallerDetection.java
├── CompositeLogger.java
├── ConsoleLogger.java
├── Dbg.java
├── DbgSource.java
├── DefaultLoggerCreator.java
├── ILevelControl.java
├── ILogger.java
├── JsonLogger.java
├── LOG.java
├── LogEntry.java
├── LoggerIntrospection.java
├── MemoryLogger.java
├── ShortStackTrace.java
├── Slf4jLogger.java
└── package-info.java
```

- `LOG` — the static entry point with all the `trace` / `debug` / `info` / `warn` / `error` overloads and `dbg`.
- `ILogger` — the extension point: one abstract method plus an optional level filter.
- `LogEntry` — one log record and the message formatter.
- `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger`, `Slf4jLogger` — the bundled implementations: text, JSON lines and the bridge to SLF4J.
- `MemoryLogger`, `CompositeLogger` — capturing entries in tests and sending them to several loggers.
- `DefaultLoggerCreator` — picks the logger at startup from a system property or a properties file.

The latest stable version is **1.3**; the version under development is **1.4-SNAPSHOT** (see [Changelog](#changelog)).

## Installation

**Maven (pom.xml)**

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>com.nanolaba</groupId>
    <artifactId>nanolog</artifactId>
    <version>1.3</version>
</dependency>
```

**Gradle (build.gradle)**

```groovy
dependencies {
    implementation 'com.nanolaba:nanolog:1.3'
}
```

<details>
<summary>Manual download</summary>

Get the JAR from [Maven Central](https://repo1.maven.org/maven2/com/nanolaba/nanolog/1.3) and add it to the classpath.

</details>

Requirements: Java 8+. The jar declares `Automatic-Module-Name: com.nanolaba.nanolog` for modular applications.

## Quick start

No setup is needed: `ConsoleLogger` is active by default and prints every level, including `TRACE`.

```java
public static void main(String[] args) {
    // No logger field: the source class is detected automatically
    LOG.info("Application started");

    // SLF4J-style {} placeholders
    LOG.debug("Loaded {} items in {} ms", 42, 17);

    // Lazy message: the lambda runs only if DEBUG is enabled
    LOG.debug(() -> "Expensive report: " + buildReport());

    // The source class can also be passed explicitly
    LOG.warn(QuickStart.class, "Disk space is low");

    String input = "not a number";
    try {
        Integer.parseInt(input);
    } catch (NumberFormatException e) {
        // Exception plus a parameterized message; the stack trace follows the message
        LOG.error(e, "Failed to parse \"{}\"", input);
    }
}
```

Console output (`ERROR` goes to `System.err`, everything else to `System.out`):

```
INFO 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Application started
DEBUG 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Loaded 42 items in 17 ms
DEBUG 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Expensive report: ...
WARN 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Disk space is low
ERROR 10.11.2026 21:30:00 [QuickStart] Failed to parse "not a number"
java.lang.NumberFormatException: For input string: "not a number"
	at java.lang.NumberFormatException.forInputString(NumberFormatException.java:65)
	...
```

### API at a glance

Every level has the same set of overloads; `info` below stands for `trace`, `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error`.

| Call | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `LOG.info(message)` | any object; its `toString()` is called safely |
| `LOG.info("... {} ...", args)` | parameterized message, see [Message formatting](#message-formatting) |
| `LOG.info(() -> message)` | lazy message, evaluated only if the level is enabled |
| `LOG.info(throwable)` | stack trace without a message |
| `LOG.info(throwable, message)` | message plus stack trace; the message may also be a `Supplier` |
| `LOG.info(throwable, "... {} ...", args)` | exception plus a parameterized message |
| `LOG.info("... {} ...", args, throwable)` | the SLF4J order: a trailing exception that no `{}` consumes becomes the exception of the entry |
| `LOG.info(SomeClass.class, ...)` | any form above with an explicit source class |
| `LOG.isInfoEnabled()` | level check, with or without an explicit class |
| `LOG.setLevel(level)`, `LOG.setLevel("com.acme", level)` | change the global level or the level of a package while the application runs, see [Changing levels at run time](#changing-levels-at-run-time) |
| `LOG.withLevel("com.acme", level)` | the same for a `try` block, restored at its end |
| `LOG.dbg(expression)` | print the expression, its value and the call site, and return the value, see [Print debugging](#print-debugging-logdbg-prints-the-expression-and-its-value) |
| `LOG.once().warn(...)` | log a statement only the first time it runs, see [Rate limiting](#rate-limiting) |
| `LOG.atMostEvery(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).warn(...)` | at most once per period, with the number of skipped calls on the next entry |
| `LOG.log(level, sourceClass, throwable, supplier, args)` | the universal entry point every overload delegates to |

Every class and method is documented in the [Javadoc](https://javadoc.io/doc/com.nanolaba/nanolog/1.3), which IDEs also show from the sources jar.

## Print debugging: `LOG.dbg` prints the expression and its value

`LOG.dbg(...)` is the Java counterpart of Rust's `dbg!` and Python's icecream: it prints the expression as written in the source, its value and type, and the file and line of the call, and returns the value, so it wraps any expression in place. Since 1.4.

```java
BigDecimal total = LOG.dbg(order.total());   // prints, then returns the value
LOG.dbg(user, cart.size());
LOG.dbg();                                   // prints "reached"
```

```
DBG 17.11.2026 10:15:02 [PrintDebugging.checkout(PrintDebugging.java:21)] order.total() = 129.90 (BigDecimal)
DBG 17.11.2026 10:15:02 [PrintDebugging.checkout(PrintDebugging.java:22)] user = "alice", cart.size() = 3 (Integer)
DBG 17.11.2026 10:15:02 [PrintDebugging.checkout(PrintDebugging.java:23)] reached
```

- The text comes from the source file of the call site. The source directory is derived from where the class was loaded: `target/classes` leads to `src/main/java`, `target/test-classes` to `src/test/java`, Gradle's `build/classes/java/main` to `src/main/java`, and the same for Kotlin; for other layouts the usual directories of the working directory are tried. `nanolog.sources=dir1,dir2` names them explicitly. Each call site is read once, arguments spread over several lines included.
- Without the text only the values are printed, never an error: when no source directory is found (a production jar), the source file is newer than its class, or the line holds two `dbg` calls, since Java reports the line of a call but not its column.
- Strings and chars are quoted and escaped, so a value never breaks the line; arrays are printed element by element; other values are followed by their type, unless their text starts with it, as `User{id=17}` does.
- It is a `DEBUG` entry: `nanolog.level` and package rules apply, and a level that is off everywhere costs no stack walk. `ConsoleLogger` marks it `DBG` and prints the call site even without `showLocation`, `JsonLogger` adds `"dbg":true`, any logger tells it apart with `LogEntry.isDbg()`. `LOG.once().dbg(...)` and `LOG.atMostEvery(...).dbg(...)` limit it like any other statement.
- `dbg` is meant to be temporary, for you and for a coding agent alike: a debug print that names its values replaces a series of `System.out.println` calls, and its distinct name is easy to find and remove before a commit (`grep -rn "LOG.dbg("`).

Rust has had `dbg!` in its standard library since 1.32 (2019), Python has had `f"{x=}"` since 3.8 and the icecream package; the JDK has nothing comparable, and an IDE template such as IntelliJ's `soutv` types the name into the code, where it goes stale on a rename.

## Agent-driven development

When a coding agent (Claude Code, Codex, Copilot and others) writes and debugs the code,
one short loop repeats many times: edit, run, read the output, edit again.
**Nanolog** keeps every step of that loop cheap.

- **One line to add logging.** No logger field and no `getLogger(Foo.class)` that has to match the class name: one import and `LOG.info(...)`. The diff is a single line, and nothing goes stale when the code is moved or the class is renamed.
- **Output from the first run.** `ConsoleLogger` works without configuration and prints every level, `TRACE` included. A `LOG.debug(...)` added while investigating a problem is visible in the very next run, with no backend to set up first.
- **Levels per run, without code.** `NANOLOG_LEVEL=INFO` cuts the noise once the first run is read, and `-Dnanolog.level.com.acme.payments=DEBUG` turns detail up for one package, even if the startup code switched `DEBUG` off. Agents in sandboxes and CI can always set an environment variable; a temporary code edit, by contrast, tends to get committed. See [Levels and options without code](#levels-and-options-without-code).
- **Lines that are easy to read back.** One entry is one line of the form `LEVEL date [SourceClass] message`, followed by the stack trace if there is one. The output is simple to `grep` and to match against the sources. With `setShowLocation(true)` every line also names the method and the line of the call, `[PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87)]`, so the agent jumps from the output straight to the statement. Through SLF4J, the backend's own `%file:%line` reports the same call site.
- **Output a script can parse.** `-Dnanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.JsonLogger` switches to one JSON object per line, with the timestamp, thread, call site and stack trace as fields, ready for `jq` or a script the agent writes on the fly. See [JsonLogger](#jsonlogger).
- **SLF4J habits carry over.** The same `{}` placeholders, and the exception may go first or last: `LOG.error("Failed to load {}", id, e)` logs the stack trace exactly as SLF4J does.
- **A log call cannot fail the run.** Logging never throws: a broken `toString()`, a lazy message whose lambda throws, a `null` or a wrong number of `{}` arguments ends up as a readable message, not as an exception. A log statement is never the reason a test turns red. In test runs, `-Dnanolog.strict=true` still reports such mismatches with the call site, so they get fixed instead of staying silent.
- **Repeated lines do not crowd out the rest.** A retry loop or a full queue can print the same line thousands of times and push the line that matters out of the context window. `LOG.once()` and `LOG.atMostEvery(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)` keep such a statement to one line, and the next one that gets through says `[skipped 241]`; see [Rate limiting](#rate-limiting).
- **The whole library fits in a context window.** One package of small classes, one entry point, this README and the [Javadoc](https://javadoc.io/doc/com.nanolaba/nanolog/1.3). Every public method has Javadoc, so the IDE and the sources jar give the same answers as this file. An agent reads everything it needs in one pass and does not have to map a framework first.
- **Capturing the log in a test takes one line.** `try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install())` keeps the entries in memory and puts the previous logger back afterwards, so what was logged is asserted without a mocking framework; see [MemoryLogger and CompositeLogger](#memorylogger-and-compositelogger).
- **The repository itself is ready for agents.** [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) describes the build, the invariants and the test requirements (JUnit plus 100% mutation coverage), so an agent can fix and extend **Nanolog**, not only use it.

### Using Nanolog from a coding agent

Two files give an agent the rules of the library in a few hundred lines, without the explanations of this README:

- [`llms.txt`](llms.txt) — a cheat sheet in the [llms.txt](https://llmstxt.org/) format: coordinates, call shapes, the rules that differ from SLF4J, settings without code changes and the test recipe.
- [`skills/nanolog/SKILL.md`](skills/nanolog/SKILL.md) — the same guide as an agent skill, which the agent loads by itself when it works on code that logs through Nanolog. For Claude Code, put it into the project:

Without installing anything, one paragraph in `AGENTS.md` (or `CLAUDE.md`) of the project is enough:

```markdown
## Logging

This project logs with Nanolog (com.nanolaba:nanolog). Before adding or changing log calls,
read https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nanolaba/nanolog/main/llms.txt
```

Both files are generated from `agent-guide.src.md` on every build: the versions come from `pom.xml`, the code
from the compiled examples, and CI fails when they are stale. Ideas for making the library easier for agents
are collected under the [`agents` label](https://github.com/nanolaba/nanolog/issues?q=is%3Aissue+label%3Aagents).

## Choosing a logger

The default `ConsoleLogger` can be replaced in three ways:

1. **Programmatically** — pass any `ILogger` implementation to `LOG.init(...)` at application startup:

   ```java
   LOG.init(new Slf4jLogger());
   ```

2. **Via a system property** — the fully qualified name of a class with a public no-arg constructor:

   ```
   -Dnanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.Slf4jLogger
   ```

3. **Via a configuration file** — put `nanolog.properties` on the classpath:

   ```properties
   nanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.Slf4jLogger
   ```

   When `LOG` initialises, the keys of the file with the `nanolog.` prefix are copied
   into system properties without overwriting the ones already set via `-D` or an environment variable.
   Other keys are ignored. The file path can be overridden with the `nanolog.config` property.

Every property can also be set as an environment variable: upper case, dots replaced by underscores, so `nanolog.logger` becomes `NANOLOG_LOGGER`.
Precedence, highest first: `LOG.init(logger)` → `-Dnanolog.logger` → `NANOLOG_LOGGER` → `nanolog.properties` → `ConsoleLogger`.
A no-argument `LOG.init()` re-reads the property and the file.

| Property | Meaning | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `nanolog.logger` | class name of the `ILogger` implementation | `com.nanolaba.logging.ConsoleLogger` |
| `nanolog.config` | classpath resource with the configuration | `nanolog.properties` |
| `nanolog.sources` | source directories that `LOG.dbg` reads the text of its arguments from, comma-separated; empty turns the reading off | derived from the class location |
| `nanolog.strict` | report calls whose `{}` placeholders and arguments do not match, see [Message formatting](#message-formatting) | `false` |

If the class named in `nanolog.logger` cannot be instantiated, **Nanolog** prints a
`[NANOLOG]`-prefixed diagnostic to `System.err` and carries on with `ConsoleLogger`.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> `LOG.init` replaces the logger for the whole JVM. Call it once at application startup, before other threads start logging. Any library on the classpath can call it as well, so do not call it from library code.

### ConsoleLogger

The default implementation. Writes `ERROR` to `System.err` and everything else to `System.out`, one line per entry plus the stack trace:

```
LEVEL dd.MM.yyyy HH:mm:ss [SourceClass] Message
```

Every component is controlled by a fluent setter:

```java
LOG.init(new ConsoleLogger()
        .setShowLevel(true)
        .setShowDate(true)
        .setDateFormat(new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd HH:mm:ss.SSS"))
        .setShowSource(true)
        .setShowSourceFullName(false)
        .setShowLocation(false)
        .setShowThread(false)
        .setStream("err@ERROR")
        .setTraceEnabled(false)
        .setDebugEnabled(false));
```

- `showLevel` — the level name.
- `showDate` + `dateFormat` — the timestamp and its `SimpleDateFormat`; formatting is synchronized, so one shared format is safe.
- `showSource` / `showSourceFullName` — the simple or the fully qualified source class name. An anonymous or local class passed explicitly has no such name and is shown by its binary name, `Foo$1` or `com.acme.Foo$1`.
- `showLocation` — the call site after the class name, in the form stack traces use, so IDEs and terminals turn it into a link: `[PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87)]`. Off by default. A call with an explicit source class has no call site and keeps the plain `[PaymentService]`.
- `showThread` — the name of the thread that logged, in square brackets after the date: `[main]`, `[pool-1-thread-3]`. Off by default; with a thread pool it tells the interleaved lines of different tasks apart. `JsonLogger` always writes the thread.
- `stream` — which levels go to `System.err`: `err@ERROR` (the default) sends only errors there, `err@WARN` warnings and errors, `err` everything, `out` nothing. One stream keeps errors in a pipe and keeps the order of the lines when standard output and standard error are captured apart.
- `exceptionExclude` / `exceptionMaxFrames` — shorter stack traces, see [Shorter stack traces](#shorter-stack-traces).
- `traceEnabled` … `errorEnabled` — per-level switches; everything is enabled by default, so switch `TRACE` and `DEBUG` off in production, in code or with `nanolog.level=INFO`. Disabled levels are rejected before the `LogEntry` is built, so lazy messages are never evaluated. `setLevel(level)` sets all five at once, and the switches may change while other threads log; see [Changing levels at run time](#changing-levels-at-run-time).

For a custom layout (colours, JSON, a different order) extend `ConsoleLogger` and
override `getOutputStream`, `writeLevel`, `writeDate`, `writeSource`, `writeMessage`,
`writeThrowable` or `addDelimiter`.

### Levels and options without code

The constructor of `ConsoleLogger` reads these settings from system properties, environment variables and `nanolog.properties`, in this order of precedence:

| Property | Environment variable | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `nanolog.level` | `NANOLOG_LEVEL` | the lowest enabled level: `TRACE` (default), `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`, `OFF` |
| `nanolog.level.<package or class>` | — | the level for one package or class |
| `nanolog.levels` | `NANOLOG_LEVELS` | several such rules in one value: `com.acme.payments=DEBUG,com.acme.db=TRACE` |
| `nanolog.console.showLevel` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWLEVEL` | `true` or `false`, like the setter |
| `nanolog.console.showDate` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWDATE` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showSource` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWSOURCE` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showSourceFullName` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWSOURCEFULLNAME` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showLocation` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWLOCATION` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.showThread` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_SHOWTHREAD` | the same |
| `nanolog.console.stream` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_STREAM` | `out`, `err` or `err@LEVEL` (default `err@ERROR`), like the setter |
| `nanolog.console.dateFormat` | `NANOLOG_CONSOLE_DATEFORMAT` | a `SimpleDateFormat` pattern |
| `nanolog.exception.exclude` | `NANOLOG_EXCEPTION_EXCLUDE` | package or class prefixes whose stack frames are collapsed, comma-separated |
| `nanolog.exception.maxFrames` | `NANOLOG_EXCEPTION_MAXFRAMES` | the most stack frames per throwable; `0` (default) for no limit |

```
java -Dnanolog.level=WARN -Dnanolog.level.com.acme.payments=DEBUG -jar app.jar
NANOLOG_LEVEL=WARN NANOLOG_LEVELS=com.acme.payments=DEBUG java -jar app.jar
```

- A package or class rule beats the global level, however that level was set, setters included. Turning `DEBUG` on for one package therefore needs no code change.
- The most specific rule wins: the class itself, then its enclosing classes, then its packages from the innermost outwards. A rule matches whole name segments only, so `com.acme.pay` does not cover `com.acme.payments`.
- `nanolog.level.<name>` beats an item for the same name in `nanolog.levels`.
- Setters called after the constructor override the values it read, so `new ConsoleLogger().setDebugEnabled(false)` in code wins over `nanolog.level`; package and class rules still apply on top.
- An invalid value prints a `[NANOLOG]` diagnostic to `System.err` and is ignored; logging goes on. A diagnostic is always one line: control characters in the value it repeats are printed as escapes such as `\u000a`.
- `nanolog.properties` is read when `LOG` initialises, so a `ConsoleLogger` created before that sees only `-D` and the environment.

### Changing levels at run time

The levels of `ConsoleLogger` and `JsonLogger` can change while the application runs, for a verbose mode, an admin endpoint or a test:

```java
LOG.setLevel(LogEntryLevel.INFO);                         // the global level
LOG.setLevel("com.acme.payments", LogEntryLevel.DEBUG);   // one package or class, like nanolog.level.<name>
LOG.setLevel("com.acme.noisy", "OFF");                    // a string, as in the settings: OFF works too
LOG.clearLevel("com.acme.payments");                      // the global level applies to it again
LOG.resetLevels();                                        // back to -D, the environment and nanolog.properties

try (LOG.LevelOverride ignored = LOG.withLevel("com.acme", LogEntryLevel.TRACE)) {
    // TRACE for com.acme until the block ends
}
```

- A change takes effect on the next logging call in every thread, threads that are already running included.
- A level set for a package or class works exactly like `nanolog.level.<name>`: it beats the global level, and the most specific rule wins. `LOG.setLevel(level)` changes only the global level and leaves such rules alone.
- `LOG.withLevel(...)` restores the rule the name had when the `try` block ends, also when it ends with an exception. The change is JVM-wide, not limited to the current thread. Nested overrides of the same name restore correctly when they close in reverse order, as try-with-resources does.
- `LOG.resetLevels()` reads `nanolog.level`, `nanolog.levels` and `nanolog.level.<name>` again: from `-D` and the environment as they are now, from `nanolog.properties` as it was loaded at startup. It undoes every change made at run time, the level setters of `ConsoleLogger` included; the display options stay as they are.
- `CompositeLogger` passes each change to those of its delegates that support it. The other loggers have no levels to change: `Slf4jLogger` takes them from the SLF4J backend, and `MemoryLogger` captures everything. When such a logger is installed directly, the first call prints one `[NANOLOG]` line and nothing changes.
- A level may also be given as a string, as in the settings: `TRACE` to `OFF`, ignoring case. `LOG.setLevel("com.acme.noisy", "OFF")` switches a package off, and a value from a request or a command line needs no parsing of your own.
- A `null` or blank name and a `null` or unknown level print a `[NANOLOG]` diagnostic and change nothing.
- The same methods exist on `ConsoleLogger` and `CompositeLogger`. A custom logger supports `LOG.setLevel(...)` by implementing `ILevelControl`.

### Shorter stack traces

Most frames of a stack trace carry no signal: test runners, reflection, proxies. Two settings shorten the traces that `ConsoleLogger` and `JsonLogger` print:

```
-Dnanolog.exception.exclude=org.junit,sun.reflect,jdk.internal.reflect,java.lang.reflect -Dnanolog.exception.maxFrames=40
```

```
java.lang.IllegalStateException: connection refused
	at com.acme.OrderService.load(OrderService.java:87)
	at com.acme.OrderServiceTest.loads(OrderServiceTest.java:21)
	... 68 frames excluded
	at java.base/java.util.ArrayList.forEach(ArrayList.java:1596)
	... 23 frames excluded
```

- `exclude` lists package or class prefixes. A run of two or more consecutive frames that match becomes one `... N frames excluded` line; a single matching frame stays, and so does the first frame of every throwable. A prefix matches whole name segments, like a level rule: `org.junit` covers `org.junit.runners.ParentRunner`, not `org.junitx`.
- `maxFrames` prints at most that many frames of each throwable, its causes and suppressed exceptions counted separately; the rest becomes `... N more`, as the frames shared with the enclosing trace already do.
- The layout stays that of `printStackTrace`: `Caused by:`, `Suppressed:` with its indentation, circular references marked. Without either setting the text is exactly what `printStackTrace` prints. A trace that cannot be shortened, because the throwable breaks while it is read, is printed the usual way.
- In code: `setExceptionExclude("org.junit", ...)` and `setExceptionMaxFrames(40)` on `ConsoleLogger` and `JsonLogger`. `Slf4jLogger` is not affected: its backend prints exceptions itself.

### JsonLogger

One JSON object per line, for `jq`, log collectors and scripts. It needs no JSON library and is selected without code:

```
-Dnanolog.logger=com.nanolaba.logging.JsonLogger
```

```json
{"ts":"2026-11-11T02:30:31.412Z","level":"WARN","logger":"com.acme.PaymentService","thread":"main","message":"Charge of 42 failed, retrying","template":"Charge of {} failed, retrying","args":["42"],"caller":{"class":"com.acme.PaymentService","method":"charge","file":"PaymentService.java","line":87}}
```

- `ts` — ISO-8601 in UTC with milliseconds, sortable as text; `level`, `logger` (the source class), `thread`, `message` (the formatted message).
- `template` and `args` — the raw message and the arguments as strings, for parameterized messages only; equal events can be grouped whatever their arguments.
- `caller` — the call site, when the source class was detected; `exception` — `class`, `message` and `stackTrace`, when there is a throwable. Fields without a value are left out.
- Line breaks and control characters are escaped, so one entry is always exactly one line, stack trace included.
- `JsonLogger` extends `ConsoleLogger`: the same levels, the same level properties and the same streams (`ERROR` to `System.err` by default). The display options do not apply.
- In a pipe only standard output reaches the next program, so `java -jar app.jar | jq` would lose every `ERROR` entry. `-Dnanolog.console.stream=out` writes them to standard output with the rest, in the order they were logged.

### Slf4jLogger

The bridge to **SLF4J**. Each entry is forwarded to the `org.slf4j.Logger` named after the source class, so your SLF4J backend sees the real caller, not `LOG`. Levels, patterns, appenders and files are configured in that backend as usual.

> [!NOTE]
> `slf4j-api` is a `provided` dependency of Nanolog. Add it and a backend to your project yourself.

```xml
<dependency>
    <groupId>org.slf4j</groupId>
    <artifactId>slf4j-api</artifactId>
    <version>2.0.12</version>
</dependency>
<dependency>
    <groupId>ch.qos.logback</groupId>
    <artifactId>logback-classic</artifactId>
    <version>1.5.38</version>
</dependency>
```

```java
LOG.init(new Slf4jLogger());
```

Things to know:

- Location-aware backends, Logback and Log4j 2 among them, are told that the call site is the first frame after `LOG`. Their own `%file:%line`, `%method` and `%class` (Logback) or `%l` (Log4j 2) therefore show the code that called `LOG`, not `Slf4jLogger`, with no backend configuration. slf4j-simple prints no location at all.
- The message reaches SLF4J already formatted, so the backend does not see the `{}` arguments as structured data. SLF4J markers are not supported. MDC values set through `org.slf4j.MDC` are printed by backends that support MDC, Logback and Log4j 2, through their own patterns such as `%X{requestId}`; slf4j-simple and slf4j-nop silently discard them, and the JUL binding (slf4j-jdk14) stores them without printing.
- An entry without a message is passed with an empty message, not the word `null`.
- An entry without a source class goes to the SLF4J `ROOT` logger.
- Loggers are cached per source class in a `ConcurrentHashMap` and never evicted, so with dynamic class reloading the cache retains `Class` references.

### MemoryLogger and CompositeLogger

`MemoryLogger` keeps entries in memory for tests. Every level is enabled, so entries are captured whatever the production configuration says, and nothing is printed.

```java
void chargeIsRetried() {
    try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install()) { // close() puts the previous logger back
        new PaymentService().charge(42); // the code under test

        log.assertLogged(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.WARN, "Charge of 42 failed, retrying");
        log.assertNoneAtOrAbove(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.ERROR); // a failure lists everything that was logged
    }
}
```

- `install()` replaces the logger of `LOG` and remembers the previous one; `close()` puts it back, also when the test fails. `installForwarding()` does the same but still passes every entry to the previous logger, so the usual output stays visible.
- `getEntries()`, `getEntries(level)`, `getEntries(SomeClass.class)`, `getMessages()`, `contains(level, text)`, `clear()` — snapshots and short assertions; the logger is thread-safe.
- `assertNoneAtOrAbove(WARN)`, `assertLogged(level, text)`, `assertTemplateLogged(level, "Retry {} of {}")` — assertions that throw `AssertionError` without JUnit or AssertJ. The message lists every captured entry with its call site and stack trace, so the failing test shows what was logged without a second run. `assertNoneAtOrAbove(WARN)` checks that the code logged no warning and no error; `assertTemplateLogged` matches the message before its arguments were substituted.
- `new MemoryLogger(capacity)` keeps only the newest entries.
- `LOG.init` is JVM-wide, so tests that install a logger must not run in parallel with each other.

`CompositeLogger` sends every entry to several loggers. Each of them receives only the levels it has enabled, and a lazy message is built only if at least one of them wants it. A logger that throws is reported once with a `[NANOLOG]` line and skipped; the others still receive the entry:

```java
MemoryLogger memory = new MemoryLogger(1000); // keeps the newest 1000 entries
LOG.init(new CompositeLogger(memory, new ConsoleLogger()));
```

## Message formatting

```java
LOG.info("User {} logged in from {}", "alice", "10.0.0.1");  // User alice logged in from 10.0.0.1
LOG.info("Missing arguments stay as is: {} {}", 1);          // Missing arguments stay as is: 1 {}
LOG.info("Extra arguments are ignored: {}", 1, 2);           // Extra arguments are ignored: 1
LOG.info("Escaped placeholder: \\{} then {}", 1);           // Escaped placeholder: {} then 1
LOG.info("Escaped backslash: \\\\{}", 1);                  // Escaped backslash: \1
LOG.info("Arrays: {} and {}", new int[]{1, 2}, new String[][]{{"a"}, {"b"}}); // Arrays: [1, 2] and [[a], [b]]
LOG.info("Null is fine: {}", (Object) null);                 // Null is fine: null
LOG.info("Broken toString(): {}", new BrokenToString());     // Broken toString(): [FAILED toString()]
LOG.error("Failed to load {}", "order", new IOException("timeout")); // Failed to load order, then the stack trace
LOG.error("Cause: {}", new IOException("timeout"));          // Cause: java.io.IOException: timeout
```

- `{}` is replaced by the next argument; `\{}` is a literal `{}` and consumes no argument; `\\{}` is a literal backslash followed by a substitution.
- A `Throwable` in the last position that no `{}` consumes is not an argument: it becomes the exception of the entry, and its stack trace is logged, as in SLF4J. In `LOG.error("Cause: {}", e)` the placeholder takes the exception, so only `e.toString()` is printed. An exception passed first always wins; a trailing one then stays an ordinary argument.
- Primitive arrays are rendered with `Arrays.toString`, object arrays with `Arrays.deepToString`.
- Every `toString()` is guarded: if it throws, the value becomes `[FAILED toString()]` and nothing propagates to the caller. A throwable whose stack trace cannot be printed becomes `[FAILED printStackTrace()]`.
- A lazy message is guarded the same way: if its `Supplier` throws, the entry is still logged, with the message `[FAILED supplier: <exception>]`, for example `[FAILED supplier: java.lang.IllegalStateException: no report]`; the exception and the arguments of the entry are kept. The supplier runs at most once.
- The message object itself may be anything, not only a `String`; it is converted with the same guarded `toString()`.

### Checking placeholders in tests

Leniency about `{}` is right in production, but during development it hides mistakes: a dropped argument
leaves no trace in the output at all. With `nanolog.strict=true` (or `NANOLOG_STRICT=true`), every call
with arguments whose number of `{}` placeholders differs from the number of arguments additionally
prints one line with the call site to `System.err`:

```
[NANOLOG] com.acme.PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87): 2 placeholders, 1 argument in "Charge of {} for {}"
```

- The entry itself is logged exactly as without the check, and nothing is thrown.
- Each template is reported once; the 1000 most recent reported templates are remembered.
- Only calls with arguments and enabled levels are checked. Escaped `\{}` does not count, and a trailing exception taken as the exception of the entry is not an argument.
- When the check is off, it costs one boolean test per call. The setting is read by `LOG.init()`.

Turn it on for test runs, so mismatches show up in the output that is read anyway:

```xml
<plugin>
    <artifactId>maven-surefire-plugin</artifactId>
    <configuration>
        <systemPropertyVariables>
            <nanolog.strict>true</nanolog.strict>
        </systemPropertyVariables>
    </configuration>
</plugin>
```

```groovy
test {
    systemProperty 'nanolog.strict', 'true'
}
```

A line on standard error is easy to miss among thousands; `MemoryLogger` turns it into a failing test. Strict mode hands every finding to the installed logger as well (`ILogger.onDiagnostic`), every occurrence and not only the first one of a template, so a test fails even when an earlier test met the same mismatch:

```java
void noPlaceholderMismatches() { // the test run sets -Dnanolog.strict=true
    try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install()) {
        new PaymentService().charge(42);

        log.assertNoDiagnostics(); // fails with the call site and the template of every mismatch
    }
}
```

- `getDiagnostics()` returns the findings, `assertNoDiagnostics()` fails with all of them in the message; `clear()` drops them together with the entries. `CompositeLogger` passes them to its delegates.
- Without strict mode there is nothing to report and `assertNoDiagnostics()` passes, so switch it on for the test run as above.

## Rate limiting

A retry loop, a full queue or a deprecated option can print the same line thousands of times, and the line that matters scrolls away. `LOG.once()` and `LOG.atMostEvery(...)` limit one statement:

```java
LOG.once().warn("Option {} is deprecated and ignored", key);
LOG.atMostEvery(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS).warn("Queue is full, dropping {}", item);
// the next line that gets through says how many were skipped:
// WARN 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [Worker] Queue is full, dropping 17 [skipped 241]
```

- A statement is its call site, the file and line of the call. Two calls on one line share one limit, and so do all the callers of a helper method that logs for them.
- The next entry that gets through carries the number of calls skipped since the previous one: `ConsoleLogger` prints `[skipped 241]` after the message, `JsonLogger` writes `"skipped":241`, `Slf4jLogger` appends `[skipped 241]` to the message, and any logger reads `LogEntry.getSkippedCount()`.
- The level is checked first, the limit last: a call at a disabled level is not counted, and a skipped call builds no message and formats nothing.
- `once()` and `atMostEvery(...)` offer four shapes at every level: `("... {} ...", args)`, `(() -> message)` and both with an exception first. The state of each call site takes a few bytes, without locks, and the number of call sites is bounded by the code.
- A count left at the end of a burst is printed only when the statement runs again. A period of zero or less limits nothing.

## Caller detection

When no class is passed explicitly, `LOG` walks the stack and takes the first frame
that does not belong to `LOG`, `LogEntry` or an `ILogger` implementation. On Java 9+ a
`StackWalker` does it and stops at that frame; on Java 8 `LOG` reads the stack trace of a `Throwable`.

- Nested, anonymous and lambda classes are attributed to their top-level enclosing class.
- The frame found by the walk is kept as `LogEntry.getCaller()`: the exact class, method, file and line of the call, including nested classes and lambdas. It costs nothing extra, and it is `null` when the class was passed explicitly.
- On Java 9+ the stack walker hands over the class of each frame, so the caller is found exactly whatever class loader it lives in. On Java 8, and wherever `StackWalker` is not available (a native image without the metadata for it), the frames of a `Throwable` carry only class names: they are resolved through the context class loader of the thread first and the class loader of `LOG` second, so the detection works when Nanolog lives in a shared loader of an application server and the caller in a web application. A frame neither loader can see or load is skipped, whatever the failure: a missing class, a linkage error such as `NoClassDefFoundError`, or `MissingReflectionRegistrationError` from GraalVM in a native image.
- The stack is walked only for a level the logger may have enabled: `LOG` first asks `ILogger.mayBeEnabled(level)`, so a level that is off for every class, such as `DEBUG` under `nanolog.level=INFO`, costs no walk. `LOG.isDebugEnabled()` follows the same rule. Once a level is on anywhere, even for one package (`nanolog.level.com.acme.db=TRACE`), every call at that level walks the stack, because only the class tells whether it is enabled. In hot paths pass the class explicitly: `LOG.debug(MyClass.class, ...)`.
- Any class implementing `ILogger` is skipped, so a custom logger that logs through `LOG` must pass its source class explicitly.
- If no frame qualifies, the entry is still logged, without a source class and a call site, as with `LOG.log(level, null, ...)`. That happens when the code runs entirely inside an `ILogger` class, or on Java 8 when the JVM records no stack traces (`-XX:-StackTraceInThrowable`). `Slf4jLogger` sends such entries to the `ROOT` logger.

## Writing your own logger

`ILogger` has a single abstract method, so the simplest implementation is a lambda:

```java
LOG.init(entry -> System.out.println(
        entry.getLevel() + " [" + entry.getSourceClass().getSimpleName() + "] " + entry.getFormattedMessage()));
```

A full implementation also filters levels:

```java
public class CustomLogger implements ILogger {

    @Override
    public void log(LogEntry entry) {
        // write the entry wherever you need: a file, a socket, a queue, ...
        System.out.println(entry.getLevel() + " " + entry.getFormattedMessage());
    }

    @Override
    public boolean isEnabled(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel level, Class sourceClass) {
        // called before the LogEntry is built and before any Supplier is evaluated:
        // return false to suppress entries of this level for this class
        return level != LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.TRACE;
    }

    @Override
    public boolean mayBeEnabled(LogEntry.LogEntryLevel level) {
        // asked before the source class is detected: false spares the stack walk too,
        // so return false only for a level that isEnabled rejects for every class
        return level != LogEntry.LogEntryLevel.TRACE;
    }
}
```

What a `LogEntry` carries:

- `getLevel()` — `TRACE`, `DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN` or `ERROR`.
- `getSourceClass()` — the detected or explicitly passed class; `null` only if `null` was passed.
- `getCaller()` — the `StackTraceElement` of the logging call; `null` when the source class was passed explicitly.
- `getThrowable()` — the exception or `null`.
- `getMessage()` — the raw message object, already resolved from its `Supplier`.
- `getTimestamp()`, `getThreadName()` — when and in which thread the entry was created, so a logger that writes later or elsewhere still knows.
- `getArgs()` — the substitution arguments.
- `getFormattedMessage()` — the final string with `{}` substituted.

`isEnabled(...)` is called before the `LogEntry` is built and before any `Supplier` is resolved, so returning `false` skips the whole cost of the message. It does not skip caller detection: for a call without an explicit class the source class is found first, so the stack has already been walked; see [Caller detection](#caller-detection).

To spare the walk as well, override `mayBeEnabled(level)`, as the example above does: `LOG` asks it before caller detection, and `false` means that no class has the level enabled. The default `true` is always safe; `false` for a level that `isEnabled(...)` accepts for some class loses those entries. `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger` and `CompositeLogger` implement it; a subclass that overrides `isEnabled(...)` but not `mayBeEnabled(...)` gets `true`.

A logger that throws does not break the code that logs. The first failure of each logger class prints one line to `System.err`, for example `[NANOLOG] Logger com.acme.AuditLogger threw java.io.UncheckedIOException: disk full; entries it fails to write are printed to System.err`. Every entry the logger fails to write then goes to `System.err` in the `ConsoleLogger` format, so nothing is lost. If `isEnabled(...)` throws, the level counts as enabled.

## Thread safety and performance

- The static `LOG` methods are safe to call from any thread as long as the installed `ILogger` is; `ConsoleLogger` and `Slf4jLogger` are.
- A logger installed with `LOG.init(...)` or `MemoryLogger.install()` is used by every thread from its next logging call, threads that are already running included. Levels may change at any time, through `LOG.setLevel(...)` and the other level methods or the level setters of `ConsoleLogger`. The display setters (`setShowDate`, `setDateFormat` and the others) are meant for startup, not for concurrent reconfiguration.
- A call at a level that is off for every class costs one `mayBeEnabled` check, or one `isEnabled` check with an explicit class. A level that is on for some package or class costs a call without an explicit class one stack walk and an `isEnabled` check even where it is off, so a single rule such as `nanolog.level.com.acme.db=TRACE` makes every `trace` call without a class walk the stack. Message formatting and `Supplier` evaluation happen only for enabled levels.
- Measured with JMH on JDK 17 (Ryzen 5 5600X, Windows 10): a call at a level that is off for every class takes about 2 ns without a class and 7 ns with one. The stack walk, the price of a call without a class at a level enabled for some class, takes about 2.5 µs near the top of the stack and 3 µs at 100 frames; Java 8, which has no `StackWalker`, needs about 20 µs and 60 µs. An enabled line through `ConsoleLogger` takes under 1 µs, plus the walk if the class is not given. Other JDKs and the method: [src/jmh/RESULTS.md](src/jmh/RESULTS.md).

## Using SNAPSHOT versions

Development builds are published to the Sonatype snapshot repository. Add it and depend on the `-SNAPSHOT` version:

**Maven (pom.xml)**

```xml
<repositories>
    <repository>
        <id>central.sonatype.com-snapshot</id>
        <url>https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots</url>
        <snapshots>
            <enabled>true</enabled>
            <updatePolicy>always</updatePolicy>
        </snapshots>
    </repository>
</repositories>

<dependency>
    <groupId>com.nanolaba</groupId>
    <artifactId>nanolog</artifactId>
    <version>1.4-SNAPSHOT</version>
</dependency>
```

**Gradle (build.gradle)**

```groovy
repositories {
    maven {
        url 'https://central.sonatype.com/repository/maven-snapshots'
    }
}

dependencies {
    implementation 'com.nanolaba:nanolog:1.4-SNAPSHOT'
}
```

## Changelog

### 1.4-SNAPSHOT

- `LOG.dbg(expression)` prints the expression as written in the source, its value and type, and the call site, and returns the value; `LOG.dbg(a, b, ...)` prints several, `LOG.dbg()` that the line was reached. Without the source only the values are printed. `ConsoleLogger` marks the line `DBG`, `JsonLogger` adds `"dbg":true`, `LogEntry.isDbg()` tells the entry apart; `nanolog.sources` names the source directories.

### 1.3

- Levels change while the application runs, thread-safely: `LOG.setLevel(level)`, `LOG.setLevel(name, level)`, `LOG.clearLevel(name)`, `LOG.resetLevels()`, and `LOG.withLevel(name, level)` for a `try` block. The level is a `LogEntryLevel` or a string such as `"OFF"`, as in the settings. `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger` and `CompositeLogger` implement the new `ILevelControl`, and the level setters of `ConsoleLogger` may now be called while other threads log.
- `LOG.once()` and `LOG.atMostEvery(period, unit)` limit a statement to its first call or to one entry per period, keyed by the call site. The next entry that gets through carries the number of skipped calls, `LogEntry.getSkippedCount()`, which `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger` and `Slf4jLogger` print.
- Shorter stack traces in `ConsoleLogger` and `JsonLogger`: `nanolog.exception.exclude` collapses runs of frames from packages such as `org.junit` or `jdk.internal.reflect` into `... N frames excluded`, `nanolog.exception.maxFrames` caps the frames of each throwable. Without them the output is that of `printStackTrace`, as before.
- `MemoryLogger`: `assertNoneAtOrAbove(level)`, `assertLogged(level, text)` and `assertTemplateLogged(level, template)` fail with an `AssertionError` that lists every captured entry, stack traces and call sites included; `getEntries(Class)` selects the entries of one source class.
- Strict mode reaches tests: every finding also goes to the installed logger through the new `ILogger.onDiagnostic`, every occurrence rather than the first one of a template, and `MemoryLogger.assertNoDiagnostics()` fails on them. `CompositeLogger` forwards them.
- `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger`: `nanolog.console.stream` (or `setStream`) chooses the stream of each level: `out` sends everything to standard output, so `java -jar app.jar | jq` keeps the `ERROR` lines, `err` sends everything to standard error, `err@WARN` warnings and errors. The default `err@ERROR` is the former behaviour.
- `ConsoleLogger`: `setShowThread(true)` or `nanolog.console.showThread=true` prints the name of the thread after the date, `INFO 16.11.2026 10:15:02 [main] [PaymentService] Charged 42`. Off by default, so the format of existing output does not change.
- Calls without an explicit class no longer walk the stack when their level is off for every class: `LOG` asks the new `ILogger.mayBeEnabled(level)` first. `ConsoleLogger`, `JsonLogger` and `CompositeLogger` answer it from their switches, package rules and delegates; other loggers keep the default `true` and work as before.
- On Java 9+ caller detection uses `StackWalker`: it stops at the calling frame and loads no class by name, so a call without an explicit class costs about 3 µs instead of 9 to 26 µs on JDK 17 and hardly grows with the depth of the stack. A caller in a class loader that neither the context loader nor the loader of Nanolog can see is now found exactly instead of being skipped. Java 8 keeps the `Throwable` walk.
- A logger that throws no longer breaks the logging call: the failure is reported once per logger class with a `[NANOLOG]` line, and the entry is printed to `System.err` instead. Inside `CompositeLogger` a throwing delegate no longer stops the others.
- A lazy message whose `Supplier` throws no longer escapes from the logging call: the entry is logged with the message `[FAILED supplier: <exception>]`.
- When no stack frame qualifies as the caller (`-XX:-StackTraceInThrowable`, or code running entirely inside an `ILogger`), the entry is logged without a source class instead of throwing `IllegalStateException`.
- Caller detection no longer lets an error from a class loader escape: a frame whose class fails to load with `NoClassDefFoundError`, `MissingReflectionRegistrationError` from GraalVM or any other throwable is resolved through the other loader or skipped.
- A logger installed with `LOG.init(...)` or `MemoryLogger.install()` is now guaranteed to be seen by threads that are already logging; before, a test could miss entries logged from an executor thread.
- `ConsoleLogger`: an anonymous or local source class passed explicitly is printed as `[Foo$1]` instead of `[]` or `[null]`; `LogEntry.toString()` names it too.
- A `[NANOLOG]` diagnostic is always one line. Control characters in the values it repeats, such as a level passed to `LOG.setLevel` from a request, an exception message or a template, are printed as `\u000a` escapes, so such a value cannot forge a line of the log.
- Documentation: the `Slf4jLogger` section no longer says that MDC works with every backend; slf4j-simple and slf4j-nop discard MDC values.
- Documentation: `ILogger.isEnabled` no longer promises that returning `false` skips the whole cost of a call; caller detection has already walked the stack by then.
- JMH benchmarks in `src/jmh`, built with `mvn -P benchmark test-compile exec:exec`, with results for JDK 8 to 25 in [`src/jmh/RESULTS.md`](src/jmh/RESULTS.md); the README quotes the measured costs.

### 1.2

- A trailing `Throwable` that no `{}` consumes becomes the exception of the entry, as in SLF4J: `LOG.error("Failed", e)` and `LOG.error("Failed {}", id, e)` no longer drop the stack trace.
- `LogEntry.getCaller()` returns the frame of the logging call, and `ConsoleLogger.setShowLocation(true)` prints it as `[PaymentService.charge(PaymentService.java:87)]`.
- `ConsoleLogger` reads its levels and options from properties and environment variables: `nanolog.level`, `nanolog.level.<package or class>`, `nanolog.levels` and `nanolog.console.*`. Every property, `nanolog.logger` and `nanolog.config` included, can be set as an environment variable (`NANOLOG_LEVEL`), which beats `nanolog.properties`.
- `JsonLogger` writes one JSON object per line. `LogEntry.getTimestamp()` and `LogEntry.getThreadName()` tell when and where an entry was created.
- `MemoryLogger` captures entries in tests (`try (MemoryLogger log = MemoryLogger.install()) { ... }`), `CompositeLogger` sends entries to several loggers.
- `nanolog.strict=true` reports calls whose `{}` placeholders and arguments do not match, once per template, with the call site.
- `Slf4jLogger`: location-aware backends (Logback, Log4j 2) report the code that called `LOG` in `%file:%line` and `%l`, instead of `Slf4jLogger.log`.
- `ConsoleLogger`: a throwable whose `toString()` throws no longer escapes from the logging call; it is printed as `[FAILED printStackTrace()]`.
- The whole public API has Javadoc, and the build fails on a missing comment.
- [`llms.txt`](llms.txt) and the agent skill [`skills/nanolog/SKILL.md`](skills/nanolog/SKILL.md) give coding agents the rules of the library; both are generated with the README.

### 1.1

- New overloads `LOG.info(throwable, "... {} ...", args)` and `LOG.info(sourceClass, throwable, "... {} ...", args)` for every level: an exception together with a parameterized message.
- `nanolog.properties`: only `nanolog.` keys are copied into system properties; other keys are ignored.
- `Slf4jLogger`: a `null` source class goes to the `ROOT` logger instead of throwing; an entry without a message no longer logs the word `null`.
- Caller detection resolves classes through the context class loader first and skips frames it cannot see, instead of failing in application servers and plugin frameworks.
- `ConsoleLogger`: timestamp formatting is thread-safe.
- A broken `toString()` inside an `Object[]` argument no longer propagates to the caller.
- A `null` context class loader at startup is tolerated.
- The diagnostic for a missing configuration file names the right property.
- The jar declares `Automatic-Module-Name: com.nanolaba.nanolog`.

### 1.0

First release.

## Contributing

> [!WARNING]
> `README.md` and `README.ru.md` are generated from `README.src.md` by the readme-generator Maven plugin. Edit `README.src.md` and run `mvn compile`; CI fails when the generated files are stale.

- Build and test: `mvn verify -Dgpg.skip=true`. The `test` phase runs JUnit and then pitest with a 100% mutation threshold, so every change to production code needs tests that kill the corresponding mutants.
- The library targets Java 8; do not use newer APIs.
- The code samples in this file are imported from `src/test/java/com/nanolaba/logging/examples` and compiled with the tests, so they cannot go stale.
